summaries.example: Imagine three classmates independently say that the school garden needs watering. One child alone might be mistaken. If their reports fit together and there is no good reason to doubt them, the group gives stronger support. But agreement alone is not magic: if every child copied the first speaker, the agreement may not add much evidence.
summaries.summary: Coherentist theories explain epistemic justification by looking at how beliefs work together. Instead of saying that knowledge must begin with a small number of completely certain beliefs, coherentism pictures beliefs as a web. A belief may gain support when it agrees with, explains, or is supported by other parts of the web. This approach responds to the regress problem: if every belief needed a separate reason, reasons might continue forever. However, a neat web might describe an imaginary world, so coherence by itself may not guarantee truth. That is why many versions give observations or other experience-related beliefs some initial support. Philosophers also study whether agreeing reports increase the probability that what they say is true. Their careful arguments show both the usefulness and the limits of coherence.
key_ideas: Coherentists say that beliefs can be justified by how well they fit together, rather than by resting on one perfectly certain starting belief.
A circular chain of reasons is not enough. Coherentists usually say that the whole belief system, not just one belief by itself, is what is primarily justified.
A system can fit together nicely and still be disconnected from the real world. This is called the isolation objection.
Many theories give experiences or observations a special starting role. These are often called weak foundationalist theories.
Researchers have tried to measure coherence using probability, but there is no agreed-upon best measure.
Recent results suggest that coherence may strengthen support that already exists without creating support from nothing.
summaries.why_it_matters: When we decide what to believe, we rarely use one reason in isolation. We compare memories, observations, explanations, and what other people tell us. Coherentism helps explain this everyday practice while also asking an important question: how can a connected set of beliefs stay connected to reality? The debate encourages careful checking instead of trusting agreement automatically.

important_terms.definition: A belief is epistemically justified when a person has a good reason, from that person’s point of view, to hold it while trying to believe what is true.
The idea that a belief is supported because it fits well with other beliefs in a connected system.
The idea that some beliefs have basic support and that other beliefs are built from them.
A set of beliefs that support and fit with one another, like connected parts of a web.
A problem that appears when every reason seems to need another reason behind it.

questions_to_think_about: Can a group of agreeing reports still be wrong?
What makes a belief fit well with other beliefs?
Should observations get special importance in a belief system?
Is a belief justified if it fits with everything you already believe but has no connection to experience?

summaries.example: Suppose two witnesses independently report that a person was at a particular location, and a third report explains why that fact fits with other evidence. The reports may become more coherent because they support a common explanation. Yet their value depends on more than agreement: the witnesses must have some initial credibility, and the reports’ independence must be understood carefully. If each witness merely repeated the same unreliable source, apparent coherence would not straightforwardly improve justification.
summaries.summary: Coherentism is a theory of epistemic justification according to which beliefs are justified through their relations to other beliefs in a coherent system. It opposes both strict rationalist foundationalism, which demands self-evident starting points, and views that try to ground all knowledge in supposedly indubitable sensory data. Its holistic response to the regress problem is that justification need not be a linear chain of reasons: a system may be assessed as a whole, with individual beliefs justified partly through their contribution to that system. This proposal faces serious difficulties. Internal coherence may be compatible with false or incompatible systems, and a belief may belong to a coherent system without helping it cohere. Consequently, many influential views assign observations or other experience-related beliefs some initial warrant, producing weak foundationalism. Probability theory has supplied formal coherence measures and has sharpened disputes about independent testimony, existing credibility, and truth conduciveness. The entry concludes that coherence remains theoretically valuable, but its detailed formalization has exposed limits and unresolved disagreements.
key_ideas: Coherentism rejects the picture of justification as a Euclidean-style structure with secure basic beliefs and derived beliefs. It treats whole systems as primary objects of assessment.

This is not the same as saying that circular reasoning is legitimate. The coherentist response is instead to challenge the assumption that justification must proceed linearly from one individual belief to another.

Traditional accounts describe coherence through mutual support, consistency, logical relations, or probabilistic support. More recent accounts emphasize explanation, objection-handling, or relations within a cognitive system.
Purely internal coherence faces the isolation objection and the alternative-systems objection: incompatible systems could each be internally well organized.
Probabilistic work has made coherence more precise, but different measures capture different intuitions, such as agreement, overlap, specificity, or the strikingness of agreement.

The Lewis–BonJour debate and later impossibility results challenge the idea that coherence can create justification from scratch or reliably track truth in every relevant sense. Some philosophers instead connect coherence with reliability, explanation, confirmation, or defeasible support.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory addresses a central epistemological question: what makes it reasonable to believe something? It models the way real inquiry uses many connected considerations rather than one isolated proof. At the same time, its problems warn that consistency and agreement are not sufficient by themselves. Understanding these distinctions is useful in evaluating testimony, scientific explanations, memories, and information systems, while recognizing that philosophers disagree about exactly what coherence can establish.

important_terms.definition: The epistemic status of holding a proposition properly, from the believer’s perspective, in pursuit of truth.
The view that a belief is justified through its relations of support, agreement, consistency, or explanation with other beliefs.
A view that some beliefs possess support that does not depend on other beliefs, with further beliefs justified from them.
A holistic structure in which beliefs are assessed as parts of an interconnected system rather than only one at a time.
The challenge that a reason for a belief seems to require another reason, potentially producing an endless chain.
The worry that a system can be internally coherent while failing to connect with external reality.
The claim that coherence can increase existing warrant but cannot generate warrant when all relevant sources begin with none.
A property or measure that would make greater coherence correspond to a greater probability of truth under specified conditions.

questions_to_think_about: Does treating a whole belief system as justified successfully answer the regress problem, or merely relocate it?
What kind of role should observation play in a coherentist theory?
Can two incompatible systems be equally coherent, and if so, what would distinguish them?
Should coherence be measured by agreement, explanatory power, probability, or several dimensions together?
What should count as relevant evidence when judging whether a coherent set is likely to be true?

summaries.example: You are trying to decide whether a rumor about a school event is true. One student tells you, but that student often guesses. Later, two students give the same account, and their stories explain details you already observed. The information now fits together better. Still, if both students heard the rumor from the same unreliable person, their agreement may not provide as much support as independent reports would. Coherence can help, but it must be connected to evidence and source reliability.
summaries.summary: Coherentist theories of epistemic justification say that a belief is justified when it fits appropriately into a larger network of beliefs. This contrasts with foundationalism, which looks for basic beliefs that support the rest. Coherentism arose partly because strict accounts based on certainty or indubitable sensory data seem unable to explain much of ordinary knowledge. It also offers a response to the regress problem. Rather than tracing reasons backward forever, it treats the belief system as a whole as the primary object of justification. The view faces two related objections: an internally tidy system may be isolated from reality, and there may be several equally coherent systems that disagree. To address these concerns, many theories give observations or experience-related beliefs a special initial role. Philosophers have proposed different accounts of coherence, including mutual probabilistic support, explanatory links, consistency, and responses to possible objections. Formal probability models have clarified the debate but have not produced consensus. They also support a cautious conclusion: coherence can sometimes increase support or reliability, yet it may not create justification when the starting information has no credibility at all.
key_ideas: Foundationalists compare knowledge to a structure built on basic beliefs. Coherentists compare it to a web in which beliefs support and constrain one another.
Coherentism is more than simply rejecting foundationalism. It offers a positive account: the organization of the entire belief system helps justify its parts.
A loop of reasons is not automatically a good argument. The more sophisticated coherentist answer is that the system as a whole, rather than a single belief, is the primary unit of justification.
A coherent system might still be detached from reality, and different incompatible systems might each be coherent. These are major challenges for the theory.
Philosophers disagree about what coherence involves: consistency, probability, explanatory connections, absence of unexplained problems, or a combination of these features.

Probability-based research makes the debate more exact. It suggests that agreement may boost credibility already present, but independent reports with no initial credibility may fail to create justification from nothing.
summaries.why_it_matters: We constantly judge claims by asking whether they fit with other information. This happens when checking a friend’s story, comparing evidence in science, or deciding whether an online claim makes sense. Coherentism explains why this method seems rational, while its objections show why fitting together is not the same as being true. The theory therefore teaches both the value of connected evidence and the need for contact with observations and reality.

important_terms.definition: Having an appropriate reason for a belief, judged from the believer’s perspective and directed toward believing what is true.
The theory that beliefs receive justification by fitting together with other beliefs in a coherent system.
The theory that some beliefs have basic support and can provide a foundation for other justified beliefs.
The problem that reasons seem to require further reasons, creating an apparently endless sequence.
The objection that internal agreement among beliefs may tell us nothing about the outside world.
The proposal that some beliefs, often connected with experience, have a small amount of support before coherence adds more.
A way of representing how likely a claim is, often using numbers between 0 and 1.
The idea that a coherence score is truth-conducive if greater coherence tends to go with a greater chance that the relevant claims are true.

questions_to_think_about: Why might a perfectly consistent set of beliefs still be false?
Does a belief need to add to the coherence of a system in order to be justified by it?
Are two reports stronger when they are independent, and why?
Should a theory of justification start with experience, or can coherence do all the work?
Can a measure of coherence be useful even if it does not always predict truth?
